slides.title: Lambda, Map, and Filter Overview
slides.prompt: Functional programming features in Python allow you to process data cleanly. Lambda creates small anonymous functions, map() applies a function to every item in an iterable, and filter() extracts items that satisfy a boolean condition.
slides.codeSnippet:
# Lambda Function
square = lambda x: x ** 2

# map() example
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
squares = list(map(lambda x: x ** 2, nums))  # [1, 4, 9, 16]

# filter() example
evens = list(filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, nums))  # [2, 4]

slides.title: Lambda Syntax
slides.prompt: Fill in the keyword used to declare an anonymous, single-expression function in Python.
slides.codeSnippet:
add = ___ x, y: x + y
print(add(5, 3))

slides.title: Lambda Expression Limitation
slides.prompt: Which limitation applies strictly to Python lambda expressions?
options: They can only contain a single expression and cannot execute multi-line statements or assignments
They cannot accept default arguments or variable positional arguments (*args)
They can only be passed as arguments inside the built-in map() function
They must always explicitly include a 'return' keyword
slides.correctAnswer: They can only contain a single expression and cannot execute multi-line statements or assignments

slides.title: Map Return Type
slides.prompt: What does calling map(func, iterable) in Python 3 return?
options: A map iterator object that evaluates items lazily on demand
A standard Python list containing converted items
slides.correctAnswer: A map iterator object that evaluates items lazily on demand
